text:
I found Q4 confusing because "High" explainability feels too much like a simple rule we already use for credits anyway; it seemed to offer no real added clarity compared to our current system. I also struggled with Q3.6 options—distinguishing between using data just to improve fairness versus accepting it regardless felt blurred when the primary goal is actually helping struggling students, not policing equality per se.

Most importantly, I believe explainability (Q4) and intervention type (Q6/Q7) are the most critical design factors right now. We saw a strong split on Q5: many agreed to trade off overall accuracy for fairness by losing just 3 or fewer hits, while others insisted we'd never accept missing more students even slightly unfairly. This tension suggests that perhaps "fairness" here doesn't mean treating everyone equally in outcome, but rather ensuring our *contact strategy* respects dignity regardless of the data point used to flag them. A mandatory opt-out mechanism might help bridge this gap between wanting broader support and protecting student privacy.

I found Q3 very tricky because I am non-binary with ADHD; knowing my disability helps me get help but feels invasive if used to "flag" others similarly. For Q5 and 4 (explainability), the tension is real: some want broad support over all costs, while we fear bias deepening existing inequalities like race/ethnicity gaps seen in our data (Q3). However, I think a mandatory opt-out mechanism could resolve this—it lets students who don't trust surveillance keep their own dignity without losing help for those struggling silently. That way, the model targets need efficiently for everyone else while respecting individual choice on privacy trade-offs.

I found Q7 especially tricky; I didn't realize personalized outreach was only offered if a model flagged someone as needing help. The group's strong preference for mandatory opt-outs is inspiring but might clash with our core goal: reaching out *proactively* to students who are in crisis without realizing it. If we require an opt-out, wouldn't that mean the system can no longer predict difficulties and offer support before a student asks? I'd agree on fairness (Q5) as non-negotiable, but I worry over-optimizing for transparency might leave vulnerable groups behind. Perhaps "fairness" shouldn't just be about statistical parity across groups—it should also ensure we don't miss high-risk individuals simply because the model is too conservative or their data was de-prioritized?

I found Q3 confusing: I didn't realize financial aid status might flag my previous dropout experience or bias against other students needing money more than grades alone suggest. The biggest tension is between accuracy and fairness; the group wants to catch me like they caught me before, but many agreed that racial/ethnic data should never be used even with a high threshold because it feels inherently discriminatory in our context. I prioritized explainability above all—I need to understand exactly why I'm flagged so advisors don't make assumptions about my "group" or mental health. If we use sensitive data without clear, specific reasons for each flag, students won't trust the system enough to accept help later.

I found Q3.4 on Absalon data tricky; I hesitated because tracking my page views feels like surveillance that overshadows support for a mental health condition affecting me specifically. My answers showed high thresholds for sensitive data unless fairness was directly improved, fearing bias against disabled peers. The tension between proactive outreach and mandatory opt-outs (S1 & S4) worries me: without it, the model risks targeting rather than supporting vulnerable students like myself who already struggle to access help. I believe explainability is critical—not just as a rule, but as trust-building so we know why intervention is needed before acting on sensitive assumptions about identity or background.

I found Q3 tricky because "improvement" thresholds feel arbitrary; I'd never accept using my disability data unless fairness was guaranteed, not just slightly improved. My main tension is with S8 regarding explainability: we prioritize trust and context-aware flags over statistical accuracy to avoid bias. While most want proactive support, the push for mandatory opt-outs (S1 & S4) conflicts with our goal of catching struggling students before they ask for help. I suggest redefining "fairness" as ensuring the *process* doesn't penalize specific groups rather than demanding equal identification rates across them—otherwise, we risk missing vulnerable peers just to satisfy a fairness metric.

I found Q3.4 particularly confusing because I feel Absalon data tracks me even when I'm struggling with my second language and not failing courses; it feels like surveillance before there's any crisis to address. My biggest tension was between the need for early, anonymous support versus mandatory opt-outs suggested by others (S1/S4). An opt-out might let people choose privacy but risks missing those who can't or won't withdraw due to stigma. I answered "small" improvements on age because knowing if a student is 20 vs 25 helps advisors understand their transition context, whereas racial data was never acceptable regardless of fairness gains. Ultimately, I believe the design must prioritize specific reasons for flags—explainability—to prevent assumptions about my group (nationality/first-gen) overriding individual need. Without clear explanations, even "fair" models may just be more efficient ways to ignore certain students rather than help them.

I found Q3 confusing because I couldn't tell if using admissions data would hurt my chances for scholarships or bias against international peers like me. My answers differed from S6; while they hesitated on Absalon activity due to surveillance fears, I thought page views might actually help identify isolated students quickly enough to save their degrees.

The group's strong split on fairness (Q5) shows a tension: some see it as protecting marginalized groups from missed support, others fear "fairness" becomes another way to ignore specific needs or mandate opt-outs that exclude those who can't withdraw due to stigma. I believe the model shouldn't just balance accuracy; advisors need full context—like knowing if someone is struggling financially beyond grades—to give real help, not generic messages we all reject anyway (Q6). Explainability must be clear on why a flag appears, but data usage should remain individual-specific rather than predictive profiling based on identity. A mandatory opt-out feels too rigid for those fearing social exclusion; instead, the system should prioritize *trust* over blanket privacy rules to ensure support actually reaches vulnerable students like myself who might otherwise stay silent.

I found Q3.4 tricky; I hesitated because tracking my page views feels like surveillance that overshadows support for a mental health condition affecting me specifically. My answers showed high thresholds for sensitive data unless fairness was directly improved, fearing bias against disabled peers or assuming everyone needs help. The tension between proactive outreach and mandatory opt-outs worries me: without it, the model risks targeting rather than supporting vulnerable students who already struggle to access help due to stigma. I believe explainability is critical—not just as a rule, but as trust-building so we know why intervention is needed before acting on sensitive assumptions about identity or background. If advisors don't understand my specific context, they might misdiagnose me based solely on group data rather than seeing the individual student in front of them who needs support most right now.

I found Q3.4 and Q6 confusing because I'm an international new student; page views feel like surveillance if they imply "struggling" before a crisis exists. In my earlier answers (Q7.1/7.2), I preferred *balance* for generic outreach but only acceptable limits or even fewer contacts for personalized emails to avoid stigmatizing specific groups unnecessarily based on my background, nationality, or first-gen status. The group's tension between mandatory opt-outs and proactive support is real: while transparency builds trust, blanket opt-ins risk missing vulnerable peers who can't or won't withdraw due to stigma, leaving them unsupported precisely when they need it most. I think "fairness" must mean ensuring we catch everyone individually through clear flags rather than statistically equalizing outcomes at the cost of overlooking high-risk students entirely.

I found Q3 confusing because I need to know if I'm struggling without feeling watched by Absalon data tracking my page views like surveillance rather than support. My answers differed from S6; while some feared invasive activity logs, I think missing signs of distress in first-year studies could cost me my degree more than an annoyance with a flag ever would be acceptable even for small improvements on identification but only if it doesn't harm privacy excessively since being flagged is what gets me help rather than stigma. Explainability remains critical to trust; I need advisors to understand exactly why they were chosen so support feels individualized not robotic profiling that assumes all Danish female science students are at risk when the model uses sensitive identity data unnecessarily without clear justification for each case specific reason beyond general statistics would make the system acceptable regardless of minor accuracy gains.

I found Q3 tricky because I worry financial aid data might stigmatize international students like me or penalize those needing more time to settle. For fairness (Q5), while accepting a small loss on overall accuracy seems reasonable given our background, the real danger isn't missing people; it's assuming all first-gen students from non-EU countries are vulnerable just because they share that trait. My concern is data usage without context.

The group split heavily on explainability vs proactive support. I believe mandatory opt-outs (Q6/Q7) risk excluding those too ashamed to withdraw, contradicting our core goal of reaching them early. Instead of blanket privacy rules or strict fairness thresholds applied blindly, we need individualized trust-building explanations for every flag. If advisors can explain *specific* reasons rather than relying on group patterns based on identity data (like nationality), the system becomes a tool for care, not surveillance profiling that ignores nuance and protects vulnerable peers unintentionally.
